correct_citation: Philp, J. D. (2015). FLIGHT Final Evaluation Report: Facilitating Long-term Improvements in Graduation and Higher Education for Tomorrow. Columbia, SC: The Evaluation Group.
design: Randomized controlled trial (i3 development grant); WWC: meets standards with reservations (compromised RCT, baseline equivalence satisfied)
population_location: 240-241 low-income students in grade 7 and 9 cohorts (program serves grades 7-12), 42 schools in one urban southeast Florida district and three rural south-central Florida districts
outcome: Total days absent from school records at Year 3
effect_as_reported: Author: group coefficient 0.08 days, effect size .01, p=.95 (FLIGHT 12.00 vs control 12.45 days, unadjusted); WWC g = -0.007 (days) and 0.007 (absences), not significant
excerpt: No, students in FLIGHT do not have significantly fewer days absent from school than students in the control group.
note: Claim confirmed. WWC g values are +/-0.007 (rounds to 0.01). Note the report text quotes control 7.27 vs FLIGHT 6.80 days while Table 14 shows 12.45 vs 12.00; the WWC uses the table values.

correct_citation: Clemens, E. V., & Belcher, C. (2024, February). Fostering Opportunities: Results of a randomized controlled trial (Report No. 18-105D). Denver, CO: Colorado Evaluation and Action Lab at the University of Denver.
design: Intent-to-treat randomized controlled trial; ANCOVA; WWC: meets standards without reservations (low attrition)
population_location: 230 students in grades 6-12 in foster care at entry, Jefferson County (Jeffco) Public Schools, Colorado (148 treatment, 82 control)
outcome: Average daily attendance rate from district records, one and two years after randomization
effect_as_reported: Treatment effect on attendance rate 0.07 (SE 0.03, p=0.02) at one year and 0.09 (p=0.01) at two years; descriptive: treatment +6.44 pp vs control -1.47 pp at one year; WWC g = 0.49 (n=116, 84.41 vs 75.41), p=0.012
excerpt: The Fostering Opportunities program led to improved attendance rates (p = 0.02). The positive sign on the effect is evidence that the attendance rates in the treatment group were higher than the control group.
note: All parts confirmed. Full randomized sample is 230; WWC's analytic sample for the g=0.49 contrast is 116. The intervention is school-district specialists (weekly check-ins, caseworker liaison), which fits 'mentor and advocate'.

correct_citation: Lotyczewski, B. S., Whittington, R. A., Smith, L., Sanyshyn, S., Duprey, E. B., Allan, M., McFall, J. P., & White, A. M. (2024). fetched_url: https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1406793 (ERIC API record) ; https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/Study/94921 ; WWC study-findings export
design: Randomized controlled trial; WWC: meets standards with reservations (compromised RCT, baseline equivalence satisfied)

outcome: Attendance percentage from school records (also unexcused absence and chronic absence)

correct_citation: Jones, C. J., & Christian, M. (2021). The results of a randomized control trial evaluation of the SPARK literacy program: An innovative approach that pairs one-on-one tutoring with family engagement. Journal of Education for Students Placed at Risk, 26(3), 185-209.
design: Two-year randomized controlled trial (i3); WWC: meets standards without reservations
population_location: 576 K-2 students (286 SPARK, 290 control) in seven low-income, low-achieving Milwaukee Public Schools; program developed by Boys & Girls Clubs of Greater Milwaukee
outcome: Regular school day attendance (absences) from records; literacy and reading achievement tests

note: Article full text paywalled; significance confirmed from ERIC abstract and WWC (g 0.199, p 0.045). Effect sizes are from Evidence for ESSA and WWC (secondary). This is the 2013 seven-school cohort, distinct from Jones (2018).

correct_citation: Jones, C. (2018). SPARK early literacy: Testing the impact of a family-school-community partnership literacy intervention. School Community Journal, 28(2), 247-264.
design: Student-level randomized controlled trial stratified by grade within school; WWC: meets standards without reservations (low attrition)
population_location: 496 consented K-2 students (251 SPARK, 245 control) in six Milwaukee Public Schools, randomized fall 2011
outcome: Regular school day attendance (number of absences) and NWEA MAP reading
effect_as_reported: Absences: about 3.33 fewer absences, p>.05 (WWC g = 0.18, not significant); MAP reading pooled effect 0.122, p<.05 (WWC g = 0.12, significant)
excerpt: Although SPARK participants were absent from school three fewer times, this difference was not statistically significant.
note: Confirmed. Not the same trial as Jones & Christian (2021): this one is the 2011 cohort in six schools during program development; the 2021 article reports the 2013 cohort of 576 students in seven schools.

correct_citation: Jones, C. J., Reeves, M., & Li, D. (2025). The impact of one semester of Future Forward on reading achievement and school attendance. Journal of Education for Students Placed at Risk, 31(2), 113-132. https://doi.org/10.1080/10824669.2025.2547228 (report version: Jones, C. J., & Li, D. (2023), ERIC ED629657)

excerpt: After adjusting for baseline attendance and achievement, block effects, and student demographics (equation 1), Future Forward did not have a statistically significant impact on school attendance (Table 6).
note: Journal article is paywalled; checked from the 2023 ERIC report version (Jones & Li), which has the same title and design; journal metadata from Crossref. Place is wrong: the sites were Alabama and rural Wisconsin, not Milwaukee.

correct_citation: Lee, M. G., Loeb, S., & Robinson, C. D. (2026). The effects of high-impact tutoring on student attendance: Evidence from a state initiative. AERA Open, 12. https://doi.org/10.1177/23328584261448132 (EdWorkingPaper 24-1107)
design: Within-student design with student and date fixed effects on daily attendance (not randomized)
population_location: K-12 students in the District of Columbia OSSE High-Impact Tutoring Initiative
outcome: Daily absence from school attendance records
effect_as_reported: 1.2 percentage points less likely to be absent on scheduled tutoring days, a 7.0% reduction; larger for middle school (13.7%) and for students with high prior absence
excerpt: Using daily attendance data and a within-student fixed effects design, we find that students were 1.2 percentage points less likely to be absent on days they were scheduled for tutoring, a 7.0% reduction.
note: Confirmed in the journal abstract and working paper. The working paper reports only the same-day contrast (tutoring vs non-tutoring days); I found no estimate of total or annual attendance effects.

correct_citation: Cook, P. J., Dodge, K., Farkas, G., Fryer, R. G., Jr., Guryan, J., Ludwig, J., Mayer, S., Pollack, H., & Steinberg, L. (2014). The (surprising) efficacy of academic and behavioral intervention with disadvantaged youth: Results from a randomized experiment in Chicago (NBER Working Paper No. 19862).
design: Randomized controlled trial; WWC: meets standards without reservations (low attrition)
population_location: 106 male 9th and 10th graders at one south-side Chicago public high school (95% Black, 99% FRL)
outcome: Days absent AY2012-13 from Chicago Public Schools records
effect_as_reported: ITT -10.3 days (p=0.041), TOT -12.9 days (p=0.047) against a control complier mean of 45 days (n=98); FWER-adjusted p=0.109 and FDR q=0.141; WWC lists days absent as significant favorable
excerpt: The effect of participating (TOT) is equal to 12.9 fewer days missed, or just over one-quarter. This is statistically significant with just the pairwise t-test but not quite significant when we adjust for multiple comparisons
note: Confirmed. The intervention is Match Education daily 2-on-1 math tutoring plus Becoming a Man. The WWC export lists g=5.71 for days absent, which looks like a WWC data error (its SDs match the discipline row), so the g should not be cited.

correct_citation: Pyne, J., Messner, E., & Dee, T. S. (2023). The dynamic effects of a summer learning program on behavioral engagement in school. Education Finance and Policy, 18(1), 127-155. https://doi.org/10.1162/edfp_a_00368 (CEPA Working Paper 20-10)
design: Quasi-experimental static, semi-dynamic and dosage difference-in-differences with student fixed effects; compares students before and after participation, against students who never or had yet to participate
population_location: Low-income middle school students in San Francisco Unified School District (fifth-grade ITT cohorts); program is Aim High, a nonprofit
outcome: Unexcused absence rate, chronic absenteeism and suspensions from district records; ELA and math tests
effect_as_reported: Unexcused absence rate about 1.06 percentage points lower three years after first participation (71% of the 1.5% mean); three-summer participants 58% less likely to be chronically absent in grade 8 (about 4.8 pp vs 8.3% mean)
excerpt: Our results indicate that this program led to substantial reductions in unexcused absences, chronic absenteeism, and suspensions and a modest gain in English language arts test scores.
note: Substance confirmed. Citation fix: the article is in EFP volume 18, issue 1 (pages 127-155), not issue 4. The place is San Francisco (Bay Area).

correct_citation: Scher, L. (2018). Examining the long-term effects of the Horizons National Student Enrichment Program on student academic outcomes (Final report, September 26, 2018). Mansfield, MA: Concentric Research & Evaluation.
design: Retrospective quasi-experiment with propensity score matching within program site; WWC: meets standards with reservations (QED with baseline equivalence)
population_location: 1,324 students (WWC lists grades PK-10; students were in grades 4-10 in 2015-16) at 15 Horizons sites in 13 districts in 7 states and DC; programs housed at private schools, colleges or universities
outcome: Average attendance rate and chronic absence from district records
effect_as_reported: WWC full sample: attendance rate 0.958 vs 0.946, g = 0.15, p=0.009 (significant); elementary g=0.24; author: elementary and middle attendance 1.1 pp higher (about two days)
excerpt: Attendance rates for Horizons elementary and middle school participants were 1.1 percentage points higher than for comparison students. The difference is equivalent to two days of schooling.
note: Confirmed. Full-sample chronic absence was not significant in WWC (0.08 vs 0.12).

correct_citation: Mac Iver, M. A., & Mac Iver, D. J. (2019). 'STEMming' the swell of absenteeism in the middle years: Impacts of an urban district summer robotics program. Urban Education, 54(1), 65-88. https://doi.org/10.1177/0042085915618712
design: Quasi-experiment with matched comparison students who did not attend summer school; WWC: meets standards with reservations
population_location: 652 students in grades 5-7, Baltimore City Public Schools summer sites (94% Black, 86% FRL)
outcome: Next-year school attendance rate from records
effect_as_reported: WWC: robotics vs business as usual 96.40 vs 95.61, statistically significant (improvement index 10, Tier 2 moderate evidence); vs other summer enrichment, not significant; authors: statistically and educationally significant effect
excerpt: After establishing baseline equivalence in attendance between the groups, the study found a statistically and educationally significant program effect on school attendance the following year
note: Direction is wrong. Both the authors and the WWC (main contrast against business as usual) find a significant positive effect on attendance. Only the secondary WWC contrast against other summer enrichment programs is not significant.

correct_citation: Holian, L., Warner-Griffin, C., & Gold, B. P. (2024). Gear Up 4 STEM: Final impact report. Technical report for Knox County Schools (ERIC ED648513).
design: Quasi-experimental design; comparison students found by propensity score matching or coarsened exact matching
population_location: Grades 3-5, two cohorts, Knox County Schools, Tennessee
outcome: School attendance rate (days attended over days enrolled) from records; TNReady science
effect_as_reported: No statistically significant effect on attendance rates (camp year or following year); significant positive effect on TNReady science
excerpt: The program did not have statistically significant effects on students' school attendance rates.
note: Confirmed.

correct_citation: Komisarow, S., & Hemelt, S. W. (2024). School-based health care and absenteeism: Evidence from telemedicine. Education Finance and Policy, 19(2), 252-282. https://doi.org/10.1162/edfp_a_00398
design: Exploits variation over time in school-based telemedicine clinic openings across schools (staggered-adoption difference-in-differences)
population_location: Three rural districts in North Carolina
outcome: Chronic absence and days absent; test-taking
effect_as_reported: Chronic absence down 2.5 percentage points (29 percent); days absent down about 0.8 (10 percent)
excerpt: school-level SBTC access reduces the likelihood that a student is chronically absent by 2.5 percentage points (29 percent) and reduces the number of days absent by about 0.8 days (10 percent).
note: Confirmed from the publisher abstract. Citation fix: volume 19, issue 2, not issue 3.

correct_citation: Murphy, M., & Neely, J. (2023). School-based health services and chronic absenteeism: Evidence from Hawai'i public high schools. The High School Journal, 106(3), 208-231. https://doi.org/10.1353/hsj.2023.a930444
design: Synthetic control method on a school-level panel
population_location: Hawai'i public high schools, 2010-11 to 2018-19
outcome: School-level chronic absenteeism
effect_as_reported: Reduced overall chronic absenteeism two and three years after adoption (size not in abstract)
excerpt: Using a synthetic control method approach, we find that school-based health programs reduced overall chronic absenteeism two years and three years following program adoption.
note: Design, place, program (a program that provides school nurses, from 2014) and direction confirmed from the abstract. The effect size could not be checked: Project MUSE full text was blocked. Citation fix: issue 3, not issue 2.

correct_citation: Long, M. W., Hobson, S., Douge, J., Wagaman, K., Sadlon, R., & Price, O. A. (2024). Effectiveness and cost-benefit of an elementary school-based telehealth program. The Journal of School Nursing, 40(3), 248-256 (online first 2021). https://doi.org/10.1177/10598405211069911
design: Quasi-experimental: negative binomial regression comparing students with and without telehealth access, controlling for 2014 absences, health suite visits and sociodemographics
population_location: Six elementary schools, 2015-2017; 7,164 observations from 4,203 students
outcome: School absences
effect_as_reported: 7.7% reduction in absences (p=0.025; 95% CI 1.0% to 14%), 0.60 days per year
excerpt: Telehealth was associated with a 7.7% (p = 0.025; 95% CI: 1.0%, 14%) reduction in absences (0.60 days/year).
note: Confirmed from the abstract. Citation fix: volume 40, issue 3, not issue 2; the third author's name is Douge (Dougé).

correct_citation: Leach, S. M., Hollands, F. M., Stone, E., Shand, R., Head, L., Wang, Y., Yan, B., Dossett, D., Chang, F., Ginsberg, Y. C., & Pan, Y. (2023). Costs and effects of school-based licensed practical nurses on elementary student attendance and chronic absenteeism. Prevention Science, 24(1), 94-104. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11121-022-01459-0
design: Matched set of 46 elementary schools (23 nurse, 23 no-nurse) by optimal multilevel matching; cost-effectiveness analysis with multilevel regression
population_location: Large urban school district in the southeastern USA, elementary schools
outcome: Attendance and chronic absenteeism
effect_as_reported: Full-time LPN associated with at best negligible improvement and at worst slight worsening; incremental cost $68,228 per school
excerpt: the presence of a full-time LPN was associated with at best negligible improvements, and at worst slight disimprovements, in attendance and chronic absenteeism.
note: Confirmed from the abstract. Published online 2022, in print 2023.

correct_citation: Martin, M. A., Caskey, R., Glassgow, A. E., Pappalardo, A. A., Hsu, L. L., Jang, J., Basu, S., Minier, M., Fox, K., & Van Voorhees, B. (2021). Trends in school attendance for low-income children with chronic health conditions: Results from a randomized controlled trial. Journal of School Health, 91(3), 187-194. https://doi.org/10.1111/josh.12989
design: Randomized to CHECK program services or usual care; final sample 1,322
population_location: Medicaid beneficiaries with chronic health conditions from one managed care organization (mostly non-Hispanic Black or Hispanic); city not stated in the abstract
outcome: School attendance and chronic absenteeism
effect_as_reported: No differences in school attendance or chronic absenteeism associated with CHECK enrollment
excerpt: No differences were seen in school attendance or chronic absenteeism associated with enrollment in the CHECK program.
note: Design, sample, outcome and null direction confirmed. Chicago is not stated in the fetched abstract (Wiley full text blocked), so the place is unconfirmed. The 'from records' detail is also unconfirmed.

correct_citation: Leach, S. M., Shand, R., Stone, E., Reece, T. J., & Reece, E. K. (2026). The cost-effectiveness of school nursing communities of practice on elementary student attendance and chronic absenteeism: A clustered randomized controlled trial. AERA Open, 12. https://doi.org/10.1177/23328584251395727
design: Clustered randomized controlled trial among 84 urban elementary schools; ingredients-method costing; multilevel regression
population_location: 84 urban elementary schools; separate online communities of practice for LPNs and RNs
outcome: Chronic absenteeism and attendance
effect_as_reported: Significantly reduced odds of chronic absenteeism for all students (and a chronic-health subgroup) in LPN CoP schools; no significant RN CoP effects; cost $764 per LPN school and $896 per RN school
excerpt: Multilevel regression indicated statistically significant reduced odds of chronic absenteeism for all students (and a subgroup with chronic health conditions) and practically significant increased attendance for all students in LPN treatment versus control schools, but no significant RN CoP effects.
note: The effect is only in the LPN arm; the RN communities of practice had no significant effect, which the claim leaves out. The odds ratio could not be checked: the Sage full text was blocked. The costs are confirmed. The author list has five names, so 'et al.' is not needed.

correct_citation: Komisarow, S., & Gonzalez, R. (2023). Can community crime monitoring reduce student absenteeism? Education Finance and Policy. https://doi.org/10.1162/edfp_a_00361 (working paper: Gonzalez, R., & Komisarow, S. (2020). EdWorkingPaper 20-291)
design: Difference-in-differences and event study on the staggered rollout of Safe Passage across public elementary schools
population_location: Chicago Public Schools elementary schools
outcome: School-level absence rate
effect_as_reported: Working paper: 0.78 percentage point reduction (11 percent); published article: 0.58 percentage point reduction (8.5 percent) in the elementary school absence rate
excerpt: We find that the program resulted in a 0.58 percentage point (8.5 percent) reduction in the elementary school-level absence rate in the years following initial implementation.
note: The citation is garbled: it merges two titles, and the EFP article is 2023 (ERIC) with authors in the order Komisarow & Gonzalez. The 0.78 pp (11%) figure is from the 2020 working paper. The published estimate is 0.58 pp (8.5%), so use that when citing the journal.

correct_citation: Edwards, D. S. (2024). Another one rides the bus: The impact of school transportation on student outcomes in Michigan. Education Finance and Policy, 19(1), 1-31. https://doi.org/10.1162/edfp_a_00382
design: Regression discontinuity at district walking-distance cutoffs for transportation eligibility
population_location: Michigan public school students in the largest fifty districts
outcome: Attendance rate, chronic absence, achievement
effect_as_reported: Economically disadvantaged students: attendance up 0.5 to 1 percentage point; chronic absence down 2 to 4 percentage points; no effect on achievement
excerpt: These effects are largest for economically disadvantaged students, who experience a 0.5 to 1 percentage point increase in attendance rates and a 2 to 4 percentage point decrease in the probability of being chronically absent.
note: Confirmed from the abstract. The author's full name is Danielle Sanderson Edwards.

correct_citation: Trajkovski, S., Schwartz, A. E., & Cordes, S. A. (2025). Distance and disengagement in middle school: Does transportation make a difference? Technical report. National Center for Research on Education Access and Choice (ERIC ED678932).
design: Fuzzy regression discontinuity, instrumenting transportation eligibility with distance-based eligibility cutoffs (1 mile grades 5-6, 1.5 miles grades 7-8)
population_location: New York City middle school students
outcome: Attendance, chronic absenteeism, other engagement measures
effect_as_reported: Yellow bus or full-fare MetroCard increases attendance by 1.5 percentage points (about 3 days); no effect on other engagement measures
excerpt: Transportation assistance in the form of either the school bus of full-fare MetroCard increases attendance by 1.5 percentage point, which is roughly equivalent to 3 days, but has no effect on other engagement measures.
note: Confirmed. ERIC lists the source as NCREAC, not the NYU Institute for Education and Social Policy.

correct_citation: Munoz, E. G., & Sandoval, H. H. (2022). The impacts of fare-free bus programs on educational outcomes of K-12 students. Journal of Human Capital, 16(4), 556-584. https://doi.org/10.1086/721376
design: Synthetic control method
population_location: Leon County, Florida K-12 students
outcome: School attendance and chronic absenteeism
effect_as_reported: Negative impacts on both attendance and absenteeism outcomes
excerpt: This paper applies the synthetic control method to estimate the impact of this program on school attendance and chronic absenteeism. Surprisingly, our results show negative impacts on both attendance and absenteeism outcomes
note: Authors are Emanuel Garcia Munoz and Hector H. Sandoval; the journal is the Journal of Human Capital. Design, place and negative direction confirmed. The program is wrong in the claim: fare-free rides were for any K-12 student, not all riders. Abstract only (publisher page blocked).

correct_citation: Kirksey, J. J., & Gottfried, M. A. (2021). The effect of serving 'Breakfast After-the-Bell' meals on school absenteeism: Comparing results from regression discontinuity designs. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 43(2), 305-328. https://doi.org/10.3102/0162373721991572
design: Sharp and fuzzy regression discontinuity (state mandate at 70% FRL); WWC: meets standards without reservations
population_location: 1,883 public K-12 schools, Colorado and Nevada (WWC n = 1,036,384 students)
outcome: School chronic absenteeism rates
effect_as_reported: Schools serving BAB had declines in chronic absenteeism; WWC: 8.9 vs 16.9, g = 0.44, significant
excerpt: Our findings suggest that schools serving BAB experienced declines in chronic absenteeism. The strongest effects were experienced by high schools, schools with higher rates of breakfast participation, schools serving universally free meals, and suburban schools.
note: Design, rating, place and direction confirmed. The authors' own effect size and whether the effect holds in each state separately could not be checked (EEPA closed; abstract and WWC only). The WWC rating text oddly says 'cluster randomized controlled trial' while naming an RDD design.

correct_citation: The SSRN paper is Cuadros-Menaca, A., Thomsen, M. R., & Nayga, R. M. (2021), SSRN 3804072 (published in Economics of Education Review, 86, 2022, doi:10.1016/j.econedurev.2021.102223), and uses difference-in-differences. The synthetic-control Arkansas study is Cuadros-Menaca, Thomsen & Nayga (2022), Journal of School Health, doi:10.1111/josh.13174.
design: SSRN/EER paper: difference-in-differences with variation in treatment timing. JOSH 2022 paper: synthetic control.
population_location: JOSH 2022: Arkansas third graders; SSRN/EER: state not stated in the abstract
outcome: Math and ELA test scores (both); breakfast participation and attendance (SSRN/EER)
effect_as_reported: SSRN/EER: modest negative effects on math, none on ELA; JOSH: little evidence of positive or negative effects on test scores
excerpt: Using a difference-in-differences (DID) estimation with variation in treatment timing, we find modest negative effects of BAB on math and no effects on English, Language, and Arts (ELA) test scores.

The synthetic-control Arkansas description fits the 2022 JOSH paper, whose abstract does not report attendance. 'No increase in attendance' is unconfirmed: the SSRN abstract is ambiguous and the SSRN full text was blocked.

correct_citation: Bernstein, L. S., McLaughlin, J. E., Crepinsek, M. K., & Daft, L. M. (2004). Evaluation of the School Breakfast Program Pilot Project: Final report (Report No. CN-04-SBP). Alexandria, VA: USDA Food and Nutrition Service.

population_location: Elementary schools in six school districts, SY 2000-01 to 2002-03
outcome: Attendance and tardiness from computerized district records; achievement
effect_as_reported: No effects on attendance or tardiness in Years 2 and 3 for any main or subgroup analysis; attendance already 95-96%
excerpt: For both Years 2 and 3, no effects of the availability of universal-free school breakfast were found on either attendance or tardiness for any of the main or subgroup analyses conducted.
note: Confirmed: no impact on attendance.

correct_citation: Cutuli, J. J., & Herbers, J. E. (2019). Housing interventions and the chronic and acute risks of family homelessness: Experimental evidence for education. Child Development, 90(5), 1664-1683. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.13041

population_location: 172 students in homeless families (mean age 7.31) in one municipality
outcome: Attendance, school mobility, reading and math achievement across 4 years
effect_as_reported: Children assigned to usual care performed as well as or better than those assigned to housing interventions
excerpt: Children randomly assigned to UC perform as well or better than children assigned to housing interventions in this municipality.
note: Design, sample, outcomes and direction confirmed from the abstract. That this was a Family Options Study site, and that the data came from school records, are not stated in the abstract (Wiley full text blocked).

correct_citation: Dizon-Ross, E. (2020). The impacts of homelessness prevention and rapid rehousing on homeless and highly mobile students (CEPA Working Paper No. 20-08). Stanford Center for Education Policy Analysis.
design: Generalized and event-study difference-in-differences; within-student before/after participation
population_location: Homeless and highly mobile students in a large urban school district
outcome: District and school mobility, attendance (absence rate, chronic absence), behavioral incidents from district records
effect_as_reported: Reduced likelihood of multiple behavioral incidents per month; increased absence rates and chronic absenteeism, especially for students rehoused outside the city but still enrolled in the district
excerpt: I find that the treatment improves student behavior, significantly reducing the likelihood of students having multiple behavioral incidents in a month, but increases students' absence rates and chronic absenteeism
note: Confirmed. The design is within-student DiD/event study; the 'comparison group' framing in the claim is loose but consistent.

correct_citation: Collinson, R., Dutz, D., Humphries, J. E., Mader, N. S., Tannenbaum, D., & van Dijk, W. (2025, revised 2026). The effects of eviction on children (NBER Working Paper No. 33659).

population_location: Chicago and New York City

effect_as_reported: Eviction raises the share of days absent by 2.4 pp (18%, about 4.3 days) and chronic absence by 8.8 pp; increases school changes (mainly Chicago); little effect on grade 3-8 test scores; reduces high school credits and graduation
excerpt: Eviction increases the percentage of absent days by 2.4 points (an 18 percent increase relative to the nonevicted mean, representing 4.3 school days).
note: Design and directions confirmed. The population is wrong: the study uses both Chicago and New York, not Chicago only. The current version is revised September 2026.

correct_citation: De Gregorio, S., Dhaliwal, T. K., Owens, A., & Painter, G. (2020). Growing up homeless: Student homelessness and educational outcomes in Los Angeles (EdWorkingPaper No. 20-334). Annenberg Institute at Brown University.

population_location: Los Angeles Unified School District, nine years of student administrative data
outcome: Math assessment scores and days absent
effect_as_reported: Homeless students score 0.13 SD lower in math and miss 5.8 additional days
